If hemolysis is suspected, order CBC with peripheral blood smear to view red blood cell mophology. Order total and indirect bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, and reticulocyte count to confirm hemolysis. Order direct antiglobulin test and red blood cell antibody screen to confirm that hemolysis is immune mediated. C
Transfuse red blood cells if urgently needed even if blood is incompatible but communication with the blood bank will help determine when testing may be complete to ensure maximum safety. C
For warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA), treatment with prednisone plus rituximab can result in remission in more than 70% of patients. B
For refractory cases of WAIHA, alternative therapies include danazol, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, therapeutic plasma exchange, and/or splenectomy. B

Cold agglutinin disease is more difficult to treat; authors of a recent review recommend rituximab with or without bendamustine as first-line treatment. background.definition: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is anemia caused by shortened lifespan of circulating erythrocytes from 120 days to less than 100 days. This is caused by an immune response to antigens present on erythrocytes. The three main types are warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA), cold agglutinin disease, and paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH). Some authors use the thermal-based classification system of warm, cold, and mixed based on the optimal autoantibody-RBC reactivity temperatures.

list.listitem: The incidence of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is about 1 to 3 cases per 100,000 per year.
It is more common in women and in those aged 75 or above.

Cold agglutinin disease was observed to be more common in cold vs. warmer climates with an incidence 1.9 vs. 0.48 cases/million/year and prevalence of 20 vs. 5 cases per million, respectively, based on a retrospective study of 232 patients with the disease at 24 centers in 5 countries.

The incidence of anti-D alloimmunization among D-negative patients transfused with D-positive RBCs varies greatly by population based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. The pooled anti-D incidence in volunteers receiving small volumes of D-positive RBCs was 64% and 84% in those receiving whole units, 26% in mixed patients, 12% in oncology patients, 27% in trauma patients, 4% in immune-compromised transplant patients, and 6% in those with AIDS.

Risk of venous thromboembolic (VTE) events is 15% to 33% in patients with WAIHA; authors of a series of 48 patients with WAIHA reported 11 cases of VTE with 10 occurring during the acute disease phase.

In a study of associations of immune-related conditions with cancer-specific mortality among older adults in the United States, authors found 21 associations with cancer-specific mortality including an increased risk of bladder cancer in individuals with hemolytic anemia (2.54, 1.68-3.82).
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is usually idiopathic (about half). See for common causes of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA).
Some cases are associated with other autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Drugs can also commonly cause hemolytic anemia, and examples are shown in .
Some cases are associated with malignancy, especially lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or parasitic disease (e.g., babesiosis).
In a case series of 1574 children undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, 2.1% developed autoimmune hematological diseases.

Cases of AIHA have been reported in association with coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) and rarely following COVID-19 m-RNA-based vaccination (18 cases, 11 with new post-vaccination AIHA and 7 with exacerbation of AIHA).
Most commonly caused by warm-reactive IgG antibodies that cause extravascular hemolysis, resulting in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA). These antibodies are reactive at 37°C.

IgG-coated red cells are recognized by splenic macrophages which either phagocytize the red cell or remove a portion of the red-cell membrane; the latter process results in microspherocytes. These microspherocytes are less flexible and can become trapped in the spleen during their next passage.

IgG subtypes can also activate compliment with deposition of C3 fragments onto red cells triggering destruction in the liver or, in severe cases, attach C5b-9 onto the red-cell surface triggering intravascular hemolysis.
Two types of WAIHA have been recognized with Type 1 resulting in exacerbation of a pathologic form of RBC senescence and Type 2 causing premature RBC clearance and a more severe form of the disease.
IgM antibodies can cause AIHA, especially if they are present in high titers and bind to erythrocytes at 30°C or above. These antibodies can cause cold agglutinin disease.

In primary chronic cold agglutinin disease, there is lymphoproliferation of bone marrow clonal B-cells resulting in AIHA. In cold agglutinin disease, hemolysis is mediated by the classical complement pathway. Secondary cold agglutinin disease can be triggered by infection and inflammation.
Antibodies may develop associated with an autoimmune diseases such as SLE, or, especially in children, following a viral syndrome.
WAIHA or cold agglutinin disease can be associated with malignancies, especially lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
Some antibodies develop in response to drugs or drug complexes on erythrocytes.

One variant is paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), in which the patient develops hematuria following exposure to the cold. This is due to a cold reactive antibody, the "Donath-Landsteiner" antibody, which usually occurs in children.

Cold agglutinin screening in patients scheduled for cardiopulmonary bypass surgery was not deemed to be useful in one study. In this study, only 47 of 14,900 cases (0.3%) screened positive, of whom only 20 patients were confirmed to be true positives. An attempt to avoid hypothermia was used in one third of these cases and outcomes including mortality and severe morbidity were similar to patients without cold-active antibodies.

Patients with cold agglutinin disease treated with complement inhibition are susceptible to encapsulated bacteria such as N. meningitidis; meningococcal vaccination is mandatory with re-vaccination every 3 years currently recommended, although serologic analysis for these patients could be considered to identify optimal timing for re-vaccination.
Signs and symptoms of hemolytic anemia include fatigue (sometimes severe), pallor, jaundice, and tachycardia. C
Obtain a CBC with peripheral smear to view red blood cell morphology including looking for spherocytes when hemolysis suspected. C

Obtain total and indirect bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin, and reticulocyte count to confirm hemolysis. Order a direct antiglobulin test (DAT) and red blood cell antibody screen to confirm immune-mediated hemolysis. C
If cold agglutinin disease is suspected despite a negative direct antiglobulin test, obtain cold agglutinin screen. C
In a child with hemolysis lacking laboratory evidence for immune-mediated hemolysis, obtain a Donath–Landsteiner test to evaluate for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH). C

Differential.Differential_Features: DAT positive for IgG, antibody screen usually positive
DAT negative or positive for C3, Donath–Landsteiner test positive. Some cases test positive for IgG anti-P.

list.listitem: Patients with autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) may have the following presenting signs and symptoms: weakness (88% of patients), fever (37%), jaundice (21%), dyspnea (9%), heart failure (5%), pallor (4%), confusion (2%), and/or syncope (0.4%).
In addition, patients with cold agglutinin disease may have attacks of acrocyanosis following exposure to cold.

Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH): patients are usually children with hemoglobinuria, and possibly symptoms secondary to hemolytic anemia such as fatigue and jaundice. This often follows a viral illness. PCH can also occur in patients with syphilis. Following exposure to cold, these patients may develop fever, rigors, abdominal cramps, leg and back pain followed by hemoglobinuria.
Order a CBC with peripheral blood smear when you suspect hemolytic anemia.

Peripheral smear: spherocytes suggest autoimmune hemolytic anemia and should be evaluated as suggested below. Along with elliptocytes and pyropoikilocytes, they can also suggest a hereditary RBC membrane problem such as hereditary spherocytosis or hereditary elliptocytosis. The presence of schistocytes suggests red blood cell destruction; consider disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, or mechanical destruction by a heart valve. Heinz bodies suggest G6PD deficiency, glutathione metabolism defects, or hemoglobin H disease. Basophilic stippling suggests lead poisoning or congenital 5 nucleotidase deficiency.

When hemolytic anemia is suspected, order LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin (total and unconjugated) and reticulocyte count. The reticulocyte count may be high or low at presentation. If the reticulocyte count is low at presentation, a rise in the reticulocyte count is one of the first signs of recovery.
High LDH, low haptoglobin (≤25 mg/dL), high unconjugated bilirubin and elevated reticulocyte count suggest the anemia is due to hemolysis.

The direct antiglobulin test (DAT), also called direct Coomb's test, is positive for IgG in over 95% of patients with WAIHA. However, the specificity is poor, with 10% of all hospitalized adults having a positive DAT.

Authors of a review found three primary reasons for a negative DAT in patients with WAIHA. These were: (1) IgG sensitization below detection threshold, (2) low affinity IgG, removed by preparatory washes not conducted at 4°C or at low ionic strength, and (3) red cell sensitization by IgA or rarely IgM alone and thus not detectable by a commercial antiglobulin reagent that contains anti-IgG and anti-C3. When WAIHA is suspected but DAT is negative, an alternative method to detect low levels of IgG sensitization should be considered.
The direct antiglobulin test or DAT is usually postive for complement factor 3 (C3) in cold agglutinin disease.

In paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), the DAT may be negative or positive for C3. The Donath–Landsteiner test is more than 95% specific for PCH, but its sensitivity is unknown. In a systematic review including 230 cases of PCH, about two thirds had DAT result showing presence of complement and absence of IgG bound to red blood cells; however, for 71 patients, Donath-Landsteiner class for 83.1% identified IgG anti-P.
See for a suggested approach to diagnosis of autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
See for treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
First-line treatment for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) is with steroids with or without rituximab and transfusions, if necessary. B
Second-line treatment options include rituximab A, cyclophosphamide, danazol, cyclosporin B, azathioprine, therapeutic plasma exchange, or splenectomy. C

Cold agglutinin disease is treated with rituximab with or without bendamustine, B Other options include steroids, interferon, alkylating agents, sutimlimab, or other chemotherapy agents; most responses are partial. C
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is often self-limited but steroids have been tried, although supporting evidence for effectiveness is lacking. C

listitem.strong: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) and mixed groups of AIHA

list.listitem: WAIHA due to IgG is treated with steroids (1-2 mg/kg prednisone orally or an equivalent dose of prednisolone intravenously). Based on expert opinion, this dose is continued until a hemoglobin level of >10 g/dL is achieved; this hemoglobin level is reached in up to 80% of patients within 2 to 3 weeks. Prednisone is then tapered over 4-6 months.
For patients with WAIHA requiring a more rapid response, intravenous vs. oral steroid can be considered.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 observational studies of rituximab for AIHA found a complete response rate of 37% (95% CI 26%-49%). Adverse events were observed in 14% of 364 patients and included primarily infusion-linked side effects (e.g., chills and fever) and one opportunistic infection.
Rituximab 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks resulted in a 22% full response and 50% partial response in AIHA associated with CLL.

Combined steroids and rituximab appear to be more effective than steroids alone. Based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 37 studies with 1057 patients, the pooled mean proportion of overall response rate was 0.84 (95% CI 0.80-0.88) and that of complete response rate was 0.61 (95% CI 0.49-0.73). The adverse event rate was not significantly higher with addition of rituximab. Few studies were RCTs.

In an RCT of 64 patients with newly diagnosed WAIHA randomized to prednisolone and rituximab combined vs. prednisolone alone, 75% of the patients treated with combined therapy had a satisfactory response compared to 36% of those given prednisolone monotherapy. Relapse-free survival was also significantly better after combined therapy; 70% of the patients on combination therapy were still in remission at 36 months vs. about 45% in complete or partial remission in the prednisolone-only group.

In the most recent RCT of 32 patients with WAIHA who had been receiving steroids for <6 weeks, those randomized to rituximab (1000 mg on day 1 and day 15) vs. placebo had a partial/complete response rate at 1 year of 75% (95% CI 47.6-92.7) vs. 31% (11.0-58.7), respectively. At 2 years, 10/16 patients vs. 3/16 patients on placebo were in complete remission. Eight severe infections occurred during follow-up, two in patients on rituximab and six with placebo.

In a phase 2, open-label study of 24 adult patients with WAIHA and active hemolysis with hemoglobin (Hgb) <10 g/dL who had failed at least one prior treatment, use of fostamatinib, an orally-administered spleen tyrosine kinase inhibitor, resulted in 11 (46%) reaching the primary endpoint of Hgb >10 g/dL with an increase of ≥2 g/dL from baseline by week 24 without rescue therapy or red blood cell transfusion. Common adverse events were diarrhea (42%), fatigue (42%), hypertension (27%), dizziness (27%), and insomnia (23%). In the phase 3 RCT conducted by these authors, of 90 patients with WAIHA randomized to fostamatinib vs. placebo, a durable response was achieved in 35.6% vs. 26.7% on placebo, which did not reach significance. However, 2 placebo patients were found to likely not have WAIHA and exclusion of these two patients would have resulted in a significant benefit to treatment.

Danazol, starting dose 600 to 800 mg/day for 1 to 3 weeks followed by a maintenance dose of 200 to 400 mg/day, sometimes with steroids, appears to be effective for most cases of idiopathic WAIHA and some cases of WAIHA associated with malignancy.

Most patients with refractory AIHA achieve partial or complete remission with long-term treatment with cyclosporin. Refractory cases of AIHA may be treated with immunosuppressive drugs such as azathioprine or cyclophosphamide. In one case series of 9 patients with refractory WAIHA, all nine patients treated with a high dose of cyclophosphamide (50 mg/kg/d x 4 days) had a complete or partial remission and all became transfusion independent.

CAD is often treated with steroids but does not usually respond. Authors of a review on behalf of the American Society of Hematology recommend rituximab with or without bendamustine, a chemotherapy agent, as first-line treatment for CAD.
Rituximab induces a 45% to 55% response rate following 1 to 2 courses of 4 weekly treatments of rituximab; however, most of the responses are partial.

In one case series of 45 patients with primary chronic cold agglutinin disease, treatment with combination bendamustine, a chemotherapy agent, and rituximab resulted in a 40% complete response and 31% partial response. Grade 3 to 4 neutropenia occurred in 15 patients, but only 5 (11%) experienced infection with or without neutropenia.

In a case series of 10 patients with CAD, use of sutimlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against complement factor C1s, resulted in a response in 7 patients with rapid increases in hemoglobin levels with no serious drug-related side effects. In a second single-group 26-week study with 24 patients, 13 (54%) met the composite primary end point of normalization of the hemoglobin level to 12 g/dL or more or an increase in the hemoglobin level of 2 g/dL or more from baseline, without red-cell transfusion or medications prohibited by the protocol.

In a 26-week RCT of 42 patients with CAD, screening hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL, elevated bilirubin, and ≥1 related symptom, 16 patients (73%) on sutimlimab vs. 3 patients (15%) on placebo met the primary endpoint of hemoglobin increase ≥1.5 g/dL at treatment assessment timepoint, avoidance of transfusion and study-prohibited CAD therapy. In addition, sutimlimab treatment demonstrated significant more patient-reported benefits in fatigue score and clinically-important changes in physical and mental component scores of the SF-12 over placebo. Nearly all patients in both groups experienced ≥1 treatment-emergent adverse events with headache, hypertension, rhinitis, Raynaud phenomenon, and acrocyanosis being more frequent with sutimlimab vs placebo. Optimal dosing appears to be 6.5 g in patients <75 kg and 7.5 g in patients ≥75 kg.

PCH is generally self-limited. Supportive care is often sufficient. Steroids are sometimes used, but the response rate is unknown. In the review of 230 cases cited above, authors found no significant difference in the length of hospitalization for patients with or without steroid therapy.

Splenectomy is sometimes used in refractory casesand initial response is about 50%; long-term remission is reported to occur in about 25% of cases. There have been no controlled studies to determine effectiveness of splenectomy and 2017 guidelines from the UK recommend rituximab over splenectomy.

RBC transfusions are indicated for symptoms of severe anemia (hypoxia, confusion, hemodynamic instability) and/or Hb <6 g/dL. Although ABO- and RhD-matched blood is optimal, RBC units are often incompatible but these should be transfused if the patient has severe anemia. Infuse blood slowly over 2 to 3 hours in patients who have been previously sensitized and monitor for fever, chills, and dyspnea.

For cold reactive antibodies, a blood warmer may be beneficial for all transfusions and IV solutions. Additionally, patients with cold agglutinin disease should be kept warm. Hydration and alkalization may help to protect kidneys when brisk hemolysis is occurring.

Case reports suggest that plasmapheresis to remove antibody may help for severe hemolysis in WAIHA. Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs of uncertain bias, including 906 patients with AIHA, concluded that therapeutic plasma exchange vs. no exchange was associated with increased remission incidence (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.15-1.30) and improved hematological parameters without increasing adverse events.

Plasmapheresis may be useful in removing cold agglutinins but does not prevent their continued production. It may be indicated to acutely reduce the cold agglutinin concentration but this may need to be done in a warm environment to prevent agglutination in the extracorporeal circuit.

A small prospective study combining a compassionate-use cohort and a phase 1 trial included eleven adults with primary multirefractory autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) who received a single infusion of autologous CD19 CAR-T cells. All patients achieved a complete response, with a median time to complete response of 45 days, although two patients relapsed during follow-up.
Refer those with autoimmune hemolytic anemia to hematology based on clinician’s experience with the disorder.
Hospitalize based on severity of anemia and hemolysis.
All forms of AIHA may be mild and are self-limited in some patients. B
Severe cases of WAIHA and coronary artery disease require transfusion support and while some cases may resolve, some cases become chronic. C
Drug therapy can result in remission or partial remission in over 70% of patients; 30% have a durable remission. A
Untreated WAIHA and cold agglutinin disease may be fatal, resolve spontaneously, or become chronic.
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is usually self-limited and will spontaneously resolve in >54% of patients without any drug or surgical therapy.

Patients who have DAT-negative AIHA appear to have milder anemia and hemolysis than patients with DAT+AIHA. These patients seem to respond equally well to steroids and have comparable 1-year survival.
Mortality from WAIHA and cold agglutinin disease is 5% to 16%.
Mortality is less than 2% for PCH and 90% recover within 4 weeks, but disease can persist for over 1 year in 6% of patients.
With treatment, remission is achieved in ~88% of patients with WAIHA or CAD.
Chronic disease may result in need for drug therapy and/or chronic transfusion therapy.
Follow up testing depends on case severity and whether the patient is improving or worsening.
Order CBC and, in some cases, hemolysis markers such as LDH, bilirubin, and reticulocyte count.

Do not follow DAT (also known as Direct Coombs Test) more frequently than once per month. A positive DAT does not help since it will often remain positive after hemolysis resolves. A negative DAT usually indicates the disease is in remission.
Patients should seek medical attention if they notice jaundice, dark urine, pallor, or other signs of anemia.

Patients with significant cold agglutinin disease should avoid exposure to cold. They are also at risk if they require surgery in which a low body temperature is anticipated such as some cardiac surgery and neurosurgery and should tell their surgeons if such surgery is anticipated.
Screening maternal serum for antibodies identifies fetuses at risk for hemolysis.
Induced abortion in the first trimester, whether by medication or by procedure, is not a risk factor for Rh sensitization.
Newborns can develop immune-mediated hemolytic anemia due to a maternal antibody to paternally-inherited erythrocyte antigens. Initial antibody screening can be performed with maternal serum.
Newborns may respond to intravenous immune globulin resulting in a reduction in need for exchange transfusion, but data are insufficient to determine benefit.
Four of four children with idiopathic chronic AIHA responded to rituximab in one case series.
